title: XDR
summary: Extended Detection and Response (XDR) is the practice of fusing telemetry from multiple security domains — endpoint, identity, email, cloud workload, network and SaaS audit logs — into a single detection and response platform so that correlated evidence from several sources produces higher-fidelity incidents than any one source could alone. Where EDR answers host-level questions, XDR is defined by the correlation itself: an email gateway recording a delivered message with an external link, an identity provider logging a successful sign-in from an unusual geography with a satisfied multi-factor challenge, and a cloud audit log showing a new OAuth grant to an unfamiliar application become one incident rather than three unrelated alerts. That consolidation is attractive because it directly attacks alert fatigue and the mean time to detect, but it also concentrates risk. A single platform that holds identity, email and endpoint data becomes a high-value target, its normalisation pipeline can silently drop fields that a responder later needs, and its correlation logic is often opaque enough that analysts cannot explain why two events were joined. Many vendors ship a native XDR that works best with their own sensors, and open or hybrid approaches exist that stitch together existing tools through a data lake and a detection-as-code layer. Practitioners should evaluate XDR on ingestion coverage and latency, schema fidelity, the ability to write and version custom detections, the depth of the response actions available per integration, and how gracefully the platform degrades when one source goes dark. XDR does not replace investigation discipline; it changes where the analyst starts.
objectives: Define XDR precisely and distinguish it from EDR, SIEM and SOAR by the correlation and response scope each provides.
Map the telemetry sources that must be onboarded before cross-domain correlation can produce actionable incidents.
Explain how identity, email and endpoint signals combine to raise confidence above that of any single-domain alert.
Assess schema normalisation risk, including field loss and timestamp skew that degrade correlated detections.
Write and version a custom cross-domain detection rule and describe how it should be tested before production rollout.
Evaluate a vendor XDR deployment against data concentration, response-action depth and graceful degradation requirements.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring

beginner.definition: XDR stands for Extended Detection and Response. It collects security data from several places at once, such as laptops, sign-in systems, email, and cloud services. Then it links related events together so that one clear incident appears instead of many separate alerts.
beginner.whyItMatters: Separate tools each see only a slice of the story. An email alert, an unusual sign-in, and a new cloud permission might look harmless alone, but together they describe a break-in. Linking them raises confidence and cuts the number of alerts an analyst must read. The trade-off is concentration. One platform now holds a lot of sensitive data, so it becomes a valuable target itself.
howItWorks: Sensors in different places send their logs into one shared platform.
The platform rewrites each log into a common shape so events can be compared.
Rules and analytics look for related events across those different sources.
When the pattern matches, the platform raises a single incident with all the evidence.
The analyst investigates from that one place and can respond through the same tool.
Coverage and data quality must be checked, because a missing source hides the story.
beginner.example: Imagine an airport where the check-in desk, the security scanner, and the passport gate each keep their own notes. Alone, none of them sees a problem. Together, they notice the same passenger changed names on three documents in one hour, and they raise one alarm instead of three unrelated ones. That shared picture is what extended detection and response provides. It does not replace the officers at each post, but it lets them compare notes instantly instead of never.
takeaways: XDR joins data from many sources so related events become one incident.
It cuts alert noise, but only if every source actually delivers good data.
One platform holding that much data becomes a target in its own right.
